Data investigation RNPDNO Mexico

The Redacted Crisis

What Mexico's registry of the disappeared won't let you see

Mexico's official registry recorded 134,268 people as disappeared or not located on 15 August 2026. For one in three of them, the public record contains a single fact: the state where they vanished. This is the story of who decides that — and of the two very different ways a person can go missing from the data itself.

The field structure above is illustrative, not one person's file — but it is everything the public registry returns for 36.8% of unresolved cases. One field survives.

1

The crisis is real, and it is growing

Start with the honest version of the number, because almost nobody publishes it. Mexico's National Registry of Disappeared and Missing Persons (RNPDNO) is usually quoted as a single figure — more than 134,000 disappeared. That figure is real: on 15 August 2026 the registry recorded 134,268 people as disappeared or not located. But it is a stock, not a history. It counts people recorded as missing at that moment, out of 407,253 records in total: 249,502 of them recorded as found alive, 23,483 as found dead.

Read the chart as a photograph, not a film. Every number in it is a status as recorded on 15 August 2026. The registry publishes what a case looks like now; it does not publish when a case changed, or who changed it. So the top panel is a census of the present, and the bottom panel sorts that same census by the year each person went missing.

Three things in this chart hold up, stated as narrowly as the data allows:

  • Recorded disappearances per year rose steeply. The registry holds ~100 records for 2000, ~3,000 for 2007 as the militarised drug war began, and ~37,000 for 2025. This is the count of records the state holds, not a measurement of how many disappearances occurred. Reporting rates, prosecutorial practice and registry coverage all changed enormously over the same 25 years, and cases can still be registered years late — three new 2014 records appeared in an eight-week window in 2026. Treat the shape as a floor under a growing crisis, not a census of it.
  • About two-thirds of post-2008 cohorts are currently recorded as located. 65% of the 2008 cohort, 75% of 2014, 68% of 2025 [1]. But these cohorts have had wildly unequal time to reach that state — the 2008 group has been observed for eighteen years, the 2025 group for months — so this is not a like-for-like comparison, and it is not evidence that outcomes have held steady. It is a description of where the register happens to stand today.
  • Older records move very little between snapshots. Comparing our two consultations, eight weeks apart, 123 records from pre-2016 cohorts moved into a located category, against 32,102 still recorded as missing. Annualising a single eight-week window gives roughly 2.5% a year — a rough snapshot estimate, not a measured rate, and one short window can be unrepresentative. What it does suggest is that the register's older strata are close to static.

Two cautions carry through the whole piece. "Located" is a registry category, not a verified outcome: it includes people found alive, people found dead, and records reclassified in administrative batches — including the contested 2023 censo. It is not a measure of successful searching, and nothing here should be read as crediting any institution with finding people. And the bars for 2000–2005 look dramatic in the lower panel but cover only a few hundred records each, so we do not lean on them.

2

Where people disappear — once you divide by population

Mexico's disappeared are not distributed the way Mexicans are. Estado de México and Mexico City register the most cases in absolute terms, which is unsurprising: they are where the most people live. Divide by population and the map rearranges itself.

The national rate is 98 unresolved disappearances per 100,000 residents. Tamaulipas, on the northeastern border, runs at 359 — more than four times Estado de México's 82. Behind it come Zacatecas (226) and Sinaloa (211): one state straddling the highway corridors that run north toward the border, the other the home of the country's oldest trafficking organisation. The states that lead by rate are the states the drug economy moves through.

This is the ordinary way to read registry data, and for one paragraph it works. Hold onto it. The next chart takes it apart.

3

The wall: one in three records is blank

Here is what "consulting the public registry" actually gets you: for 36.8% of unresolved records, every field is redacted — no date, no age, no sex, no municipality, no case status. One fact survives: the state. This is why national trend charts and state comparisons are built on different denominators, and why every chart in this piece says so.

The redaction is not evenly spread. Jalisco redacts two of every three records. Guerrero, one of the most violent states in the country, redacts one in eleven.

4

The most violent states redact the least

There is an innocent explanation for all this redaction, and it deserves a fair test.

If confidentiality exists to protect families, it should be most common where families are in the most danger. A mother in a state where the cartels read the newspapers has an obvious reason to keep her son's name out of a public database. On that theory, redaction should rise with violence.

The data does not support it. Across the 28 states where both measures can be matched, redaction and homicide rate are negatively correlated — Pearson r = −0.42 [2]. The states carrying the heaviest violence are among the least redacted. Colima has recorded roughly 950 homicides per 100,000 residents since 2015, the highest rate in the country; it redacts 9% of its disappearance records. Guerrero, at 550, redacts 9%. Chihuahua, at 548, redacts 9%.

At the other end of the scale, Jalisco's homicide rate is less than half Guerrero's and it redacts 67%. Yucatán has both the lowest homicide rate and the lowest disappearance rate in the country — 18 and 12.5 per 100,000 — and redacts 62% of its records.

The narrow conclusion, and the only one this supports: state-level homicide rates do not explain state-level differences in confidentiality. A state's violence tells you almost nothing about how much of its registry is readable. That does not establish what redaction is tracking, and it cannot rule out risk assessments made case by case, which no public field records. It does rule out the simplest version of the official rationale — that redaction maps onto danger — as an explanation for why Jalisco is at 67% and Guerrero at 9%.

So what does account for the difference?

5

Who decides a record goes dark

On paper, the rule is humane and simple. Article 108 of the General Law on Disappearances gives families the right to keep their loved one's information out of the public registry, and requires that they be told of this right before giving information. Redaction, officially, means "the family asked."

The government's own paperwork says otherwise. In August 2020 the National Search Commission (CNB) wrote to the transparency institute (INAI) asking how to build the public registry — and admitted, in its own tables, that for 77.4% of records nobody knew whether the family had consented or not, largely because the records predate the law. Where no paperwork exists, the default is silence. And in a footnote, the CNB recorded something remarkable: the Fiscalía of Jalisco had declared that everything it sends to the national registry is non-publishable, invoking family refusals it has never had to evidence.

When INAI later ordered the CNB to release a public database (resolution RRA 09082/20), the commission resisted — citing family consent it could not produce — and eventually delivered 50,204 records out of 175,371.

Journalists then closed the loop. In 2024, ZonaDocs found 4,765 cases across six states that are marked confidential in the registry while having active public search notices — posters with names and photographs, issued by the same authorities. Officials admitted no risk assessment underlies the classification. María de Jesús Solís, whose son disappeared in Zapopan in 2020, said she never signed anything and wants maximum visibility. Her son's record is confidential.

The redaction flag is an administrative artifact — a mixture of genuine family requests, missing paperwork defaulting to silence, and at least one blanket state policy — and no public field distinguishes them.

5b

And the flag moves in batches

If confidentiality reflected family choices, it would drift — a few records at a time, in every state. Instead it jumps. Tamaulipas reclassified ~2,500 existing records to confidential in two months (May–July 2025) while its total barely moved; its redaction share went from 20% to 39%, and every chart in this piece would have looked different had we pulled the data in April. Jalisco's confidential count was flat all year, then fell by ~1,400 in the last quarter as records left the federal registry entirely — months before the new recount was announced. Tabasco deleted a third of its records in a single month.

The reversals do not stop at the edge of the panel. Mexico City's unresolved count climbed steadily all through 2025, from 6,025 in April to 7,242 in December — and then gave the entire increase back. By June 2026 the live registry showed 6,086; by August, 5,915. A capital that had been adding cases for a year shed 1,327 of them in eight months, roughly one in five. We can see the direction and the size of that reversal but not its mechanism: the registry does not say whether those records were deleted, reclassified, resolved, or moved.

Step changes, flat totals during reclassification, batch deletions: these patterns are consistent with administrative processing — records handled in bulk, by an office, on an office's schedule. They are not proof that the underlying consent decisions are fabricated. Families do decide, and some of those decisions are surely real; a backlog of genuine consent forms entered in one batch would look much like this from the outside. What the shape of the data does show is that the timing of publication is governed by administrative operations rather than by when families decide, and that the two cannot be separated from the public record.

That is the version-history counterpart to section 5. Together they support a claim that is narrower than "the state is hiding people" and harder to dismiss: the registry's most basic public property — how much of it you can read — is rewritten in bulk, state by state, with no published log of who authorised a change or why, and no field that distinguishes a redaction a family asked for from one that a missing form produced.

6

Jalisco: opacity by redaction

Jalisco redacts more of its registry than any other state in Mexico: 9,216 of its 13,766 unresolved records, two out of every three. It is also the state that stopped fully participating in the national count.

From 2022, under then-governor Enrique Alfaro, Jalisco largely stopped reporting disappearances to the RNPDNO and logged them in its own state registry instead. The country now has two official counts of Jalisco's disappeared, kept by two governments, and they do not agree with each other. Animal Político put the resulting gap at up to 2,986 people. The state government's answer, in January 2024, was a communiqué titled "Jalisco does not manipulate its registry, nor erase figures."

Jalisco is also where the contradiction from section 5 concentrates. Of the 4,765 confidential-yet-publicly-searched-for cases ZonaDocs identified, 1,026 are Jalisco's — more than any other state. The same investigation found a further 2,137 disappearances between 2019 and mid-2024 that were never registered anywhere at all: not redacted, simply absent.

What the registry would not record, families recorded themselves. On 5 March 2025 the collective Guerreros Buscadores de Jalisco entered Rancho Izaguirre, a property outside Teuchitlán, and found a cartel recruitment and extermination site: clothing, shoes, backpacks, notebooks, bone fragments. It became a national scandal — not only for what was on the ranch, but because a group of searching families, rather than the state, was what finally established it.

Searching in Jalisco is lethal work. In 2025 Teresa González Murillo was attacked and died. María del Carmen Morales, of Guerreros Buscadores, was murdered alongside one son while searching for another.

The state with the most redacted registry in Mexico is also the state where civil society keeps producing the evidence its registry lacks. Those are not two facts about Jalisco. They are one fact, seen from two sides.

7

Guerrero: opacity by omission

On the redaction chart, Guerrero is one of the clean ones: 9% confidential, against Jalisco's 67%. The same federal consent rules apply there; its search commission's privacy notice mirrors the national architecture almost word for word. Guerrero is not redacting less because it has better privacy law. It is redacting less because of what happens before a record can be redacted. In Guerrero, cases often never enter the registry at all.

The state's registry holds roughly 3,800 records. In Iguala alone — one city — three family collectives jointly document 623 cases.

Those two numbers are not a subtraction, and it matters that we say so. They may overlap, and we cannot measure by how much. Some of the 623 Iguala cases are certainly also registered with the state; others, by the collectives' account, are not. Without case-level identifiers on both sides — which no public source provides — there is no way to net one against the other. The comparison is worth making because of the ratio it implies: three collectives in one city hold a caseload equal to a sixth of the entire state register. It is not worth making as an estimate of how many people are missing from that register.

The human-rights centre Tlachinollan, which has tracked the state for decades, describes prosecutors who stall investigations unless families force them open, and a forensic service that has effectively collapsed. Nationally, between 2% and 6% of disappearance cases are ever prosecuted; there have been 36 sentences in the entire country [4].

The modern searching-mothers movement was, in an important sense, born here. When the 43 students from Ayotzinapa disappeared in September 2014, families searching the hills around Iguala for them began instead to find other people: graves of the dead nobody was officially looking for. The collective that formed out of that search, Los Otros Desaparecidos de Iguala, has since exhumed more than 160 bodies. Tlachinollan credits women-led collectives — not state institutions — with the recovery of 260 bodies in Iguala, of which 69 were identified and returned to their families. In Acapulco it records a different outcome: 70 people found alive, and 55 identified bodies returned [4].

The under-registration is not history. During Holy Week searches in 2026, in Iguala and Buenavista de Cuéllar, three families approached the searching mothers to report disappearances they had never reported to any authority. That is the gap happening in real time: people becoming known to a collective before they are known to the state.

A low confidential share, then, is not a clean bill of health. Jalisco's registry hides what it holds; Guerrero's is missing what it never took in. A state can look transparent on the redaction chart precisely because it failed at the earlier step.

The two modes are not opposites, and no state is purely one or the other — Jalisco's 2,137 unregistered cases are omission, sitting alongside its redaction. They are two different points at which a person can vanish from the public record: before the state writes anything down, and after. Guerrero shows you the first clearly. Jalisco shows you the second. Most states are doing some of both, and the registry gives you no way to tell how much.

8

What this means — and what we cannot claim

No chart in this piece supports the sentence "the state deliberately hides its disappeared." What the evidence supports is narrower and, for data users, more important:

  • The public registry's confidentiality flag is unexplained, unaudited, and in thousands of documented cases contradicted by the authorities' own public search notices.
  • Cross-state comparisons of registry data measure institutional publication practice as much as they measure disappearance.
  • Opacity has two modes — redacting what is recorded, and never recording — and a state can look clean on one axis while failing badly on the other.
  • In both modes, the gap is being filled by the same people: the families and collectives searching, counting, and digging where the record ends.

That is the subject of the next piece.

Methods and limits

This piece draws on two data vintages that cannot be merged, and every figure is labelled with the one it uses. They answer different questions and carry different cutoff dates. Reading a number from one against a number from the other will give a wrong answer.

[1] Aggregate outcomes — vintage 2026-08-15 (live). All-record totals and the by-year outcome breakdown in fig A. Source: RNPDNO public dashboard API, captured 2026-08-15 23:49 America/Mexico_City. Covers every record including confidential ones, because the dashboard counts records it will not display. Totals: 407,253 records — 249,502 recorded found alive, 23,483 found dead, 134,268 disappeared or not located. Frozen with source hashes at data/publication_freezes/2026-08-15/.

[2] Homicide and state-capacity variables — vintage 2015–2025 cumulative. SESNSP homicide victims aggregated 2015–2025 per 100,000; INEGI ENCIG 2025 (corruption prevalence) and PIBE 2024 (GDP per capita). Matched to 28 of 32 states. Used only for the correlations in §4 and the negative controls in docs/methodology.md §7.

[3] Record-level microdata — vintage 2025-12-02 (frozen). Every field-level figure: redaction shares, per-capita rates, and the state rankings in figs B, C and D. Source: the public RNPDNO record-level extract via the lapanquecita mirror — 133,566 records, upstream commit 666b3e7605, max FECHA_REGISTRO 2025-12-01. This mirror stopped publishing after 2025-12-02, having released monthly since April 2025, and no comparable record-level extract has appeared since. Our copy is byte-identical to the last upstream commit.

Drift between [1] and [3] is small nationally — the mirror sits within 0.5% of the live registry, 0.1% across state-attributable records — but it is not uniform by state. Ciudad de México has since fallen 18% and Jalisco 6% against the frozen microdata; both carry their live figures in the caption. src/crosscheck.py reports the full per-state drift table.

[4] Documentary and journalistic sources, each with its own date: Oficio SEGOB/CNBP/1349/2020 (consent accounting, universe dated 2020-08-07); ZonaDocs, "El engaño estadístico", 2024-11-21 (active notices marked confidential; Jalisco under-registration); El Informador, 2023-05-09 (Jalisco federal/state divergence); Animal Político (the 2022 reporting gap); Tlachinollan, "Guerrero: territorio de personas desaparecidas" (Iguala and Acapulco recoveries, prosecution rates); Human Rights Watch, 2019-01-14 (Los Otros Desaparecidos de Iguala); Proceso, 2026-04-03 (Holy Week searches). Web sources consulted 2026-07-06 unless stated.

[5] Redaction over time — vintage Apr–Dec 2025. Ten pinned monthly snapshots of the mirror, upstream commit SHAs in src/version_audit.py.

Cross-checks: category sensitivity tested (DESAPARECIDA vs +NO LOCALIZADA moves the national count +6.1%, but Zacatecas +42%); confidential records are counted as people but excluded from every field-level analysis; 15 headline numbers are recomputed automatically against the freeze on each build (data/publication_freezes/2026-08-15/derived/automated_claim_checks.csv). All figures reproduce from src/ in the project repository (https://github.com/heliog83/desaparecidos-mx). Full methodology: [docs/methodology.md](docs/methodology.md); refresh audit and number-by-number diff: [docs/data-refresh-2026-08-15.md](docs/data-refresh-2026-08-15.md); source audit: [reports/publication_data_audit_2026-08-15.md](reports/publication_data_audit_2026-08-15.md).

Ethics line (keep): behind every record is a person and a searching family. This piece reports uncertainty as uncertainty and does not present proxies as counts.
